Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) Abstract Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), conducted in space from September 9 to October 5, 2007. On the success of SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test sample material Pyrell®, an intumescent fire￾retardant foam by Foamex was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test condition ranges was extended to include higher heating temperature and no-flow conditions, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures used in SAME. SAMER flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. As a part of SAMER effort, three major post–flight ground tests were performed: the SAMER apparatus flow tests to obtain accurate dilution ratio data, the TEM tests to obtain the 1-g counterpart of TEM samples and a batch of SMPS tests to examine the validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of a

TEM tests to obtain the 1-g counterpart of TEM samples and a batch of SMPS tests to examine the validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of aerosol particle size for the tested materials. Based on the results of both SAMER flight and ground-based tests, it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in space vehicles. Particle size distributions of aerosol produced from 5 tested materials commonly found in space crafts were identified. Introduction Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is one of the awarded Rapid Turn Around (RTA) projects, solicited by NASA Headquarters in June 2009. SAMER is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), which was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) onboard the International Space Station (ISS) from September 9 to October 5, 2007. Generally speaking, SAME experiments were completed successfully in that the apparatus developed for the experiments functio

ber 9 to October 5, 2007. Generally speaking, SAME experiments were completed successfully in that the apparatus developed for the experiments functioned well and desired data from instruments were obtained. However, there was a major problem of the SAME experiments. After the thermal precipitators returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. After SAMER flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAMER. The first ground-based test is the SAMER apparatus flow tests. The objective of the test is to obtain accurate dilution ratio data of the P-trak and Dusttrak so that the accuracy of aerosol concentration can be improved. The second batch of ground tests was the TEM tests which were conducted under exactly the same conditions as those for the SAMER flight tests so that the gravity effects on the TEM samples can be identified. The third batch of ground tests was to a SMPS apparatus to obtain the actual particle size distribution under the same condition as the SAMER flight tests. The objective of these tests is to examine the validity of lognormal particle size distributio

ion under the same condition as the SAMER flight tests. The objective of these tests is to examine the validity of lognormal particle size distribution assumption. Besides these ground tests, there were two improvements in the data reduction procedures. One is to derive sample heating temperatures from the logged engineering data so that each test can be characterized by the sample heating temperature instead of Rt/R0 as has always been used. It was realized that even two tests use the same Rt/R0, the sample heating temperatures can be quite different. Characterizing a test with sample heating temperature makes it

easier to understand the particle generation from the view point of material pyrolysis. The second improvement is to device a method of calculating the percentage of cumulative moment detected by an instrument that has a limited particle size detection range. This development allows us to improve uncertainty analysis of the results we obtained. Since the apparatus used in SAMER is mostly unchanged from that of SAME and the basic approach – the moment method – used by the two experiments are the same, in this report, these two parts – the apparatus and the moment methods – will not be repeated. What will be included in this final report are the newly added part, the improved data reduction methods and the new results of particle distributions. As described above, the count mean diameter and the diameter of average mass measurements are independent of the nature of the size distribution however, the calculation of the geometric mean diameter and the geometric standard deviation (σg) depend on the assumption of a log-normal distribution. However, there are two indications that the distribution can be approximated by a log￾normal distribution. In the cases listed below, the count mean diameter is less than the diameter of average mass which is a necessary condition for a log-normal distribution (See Fig. 1). The second indication is that the geometric standard deviations are all physically reasonable (i.e. greater than 1 (see Eq. 3) and less than approximately 3.5 which is the practical limit on the magnitude of aerosol geometric standard deviation). The aging results show a substantial increase in the observed diameters. As expected the increase in the count mean diameter is greater than the corresponding increase in the diameter of average mass. This can be understood since coagulation consists of particle collisions joining two particles. For a polydisperse aerosol, these collisions usually involve the collision of one of the smallest (high mobility) particles with the largest (high

es. For a polydisperse aerosol, these collisions usually involve the collision of one of the smallest (high mobility) particles with the largest (high cross-section) particles. This collision has little effect on the size of the large particle but it removes the smaller particles from the size distribution. This has a larger effect on the count mean diameter since it is linear in diameter while the diameter of average mass varies with the cube root of the diameter. B. MPASS Results The MPASS was included in SAME-2 to demonstrate the effectiveness of a two-moment smoke detector. Because of how they are used, a smoke detector is not calibrated for specific materials and instead has a single calibration for all conditions. The objective is to maintain a flat sensor response, regardless of the type of smoke or the particle size so the signal is proportional only to a selected moment (e.g. mass or number concentration). The approach used was to derive correlations to predict the smoke number concentration and mass concentration from the MPASS output. This correlation was made using the other SAME measurements (number and mass concentration) as a reference. A least-squares, third-order, correlation was computed on all test points with a signal to noise ratio greater than 2 independent of all other parameters (e.g. material, heating rate, and aging time). Both figures show that the correlation decreases the relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor. The resulting variance for the mass response is substantially lower than for the number concentration. Thus with appropriate processing, the MPASS output can be proportional to either the number concentration or the mass concentration over a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions. This independence demonstrates that by combining 2 moments the MPASS is able to scale its response to the particle size being sampled giving a more accurate indication of the amount of smoke present than a single moment detector. Particularly for the semi-liquid particles, this absorption of the smallest particles into larger particles is expected to have little or no apparent effect on the size of the larger particles because the diameter is the cube root of the volume. Impact of flow on particle morphology As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are released via pyrolysis. These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the reaction with oxygen. As the gases move from the wire, the temperature and species concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and convection. With the decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical s

esult of conduction/diffusion and convection. With the decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage and nucleation of smoke particles will occur. These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the condensation of the pyrolysis gases. The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the order of miliseconds or less. Over a longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian motion collide and stick together in a process known as coagulation. This process may continue for time scales of up to thousand seconds. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11). If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an agglomerate structure composed of many primary particles connected in a low density fractal-like structure. This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11). Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low

ure. This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11). Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low-gravity condition, the convective flow past the heated wire, the wire temperature, and the aging time. As the wire temperature increases, more of the sample will be pyrolyzed and these gases will subsequently condense on the nuclei leading to a larger mass concentration of the aerosol and a larger diameter of average mass. An increase in the convective flow for a fixed wire temperature is expected to result in an increase in the pyrolysis rate and thus an increase in the mass concentration of the aerosol. Some results follow this trend with silicone rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increasing slightly with flow while Teflon and Kapton decrease. A possible explanation is that holding the wire temperature fixed does not necessarily mean that the sample surface temperature distribution is precisely the same at different air flow speeds. Although these are expected to be small variations, given the exponential dependence of the pyrolysis kinet

ely the same at different air flow speeds. Although these are expected to be small variations, given the exponential dependence of the pyrolysis kinetics on temperature, changes in the heat transport environment could change the sample surface temperature between the wire coils. A case of special interest is the case of zero-flow. The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion. Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm. Assuming a cubical geometry this would correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in the 6000 cm3 piston. If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case. The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined for 11 tests by modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware. This resulted in a very high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume. As a result the total particle counts were lower than normal and the TEM grids had few particles. It is important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios. If one performed the same experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone. For the zero-flow case, the heat is transported primarily by conduction rather than convection. This is likely to result in a significant increase in the gas temperature relative to the case with 8 cm/s air flow. A striking effect of this temperature change is the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition (Fig 13). SAME Smoke-in-Drums Ground-Based Experiment In order to assess whether the size distribution of the smoke is lognormal, detailed particle size distributions were measured with a reference instrument. This cannot be accomplished in low gravity, so this investigation was performed with the ground-based engineering SAME hardware which is identical to the setup on the ISS, incorporating the flight aerosol instruments which had been returne

ground-based engineering SAME hardware which is identical to the setup on the ISS, incorporating the flight aerosol instruments which had been returned to earth. A Scanning Mobility Particle Sizer (SMPS) Spectrometer (3936, TSI, Shoreview, MN, USA) was used as the reference instrument in validation experiment. The SMPS requires a two minute scan through a range of voltages to acquire a high resolution particle size distribution; however, the duration of smoke supplied from the SAME aging chamber is at most 30 seconds. Therefore, the smoke was collected in an intermediate container which served two purposes. The first purpose was to sufficiently dilute the smoke from the SAME chamber in order to effectively stop coagulation (aging) of the smoke particles during the SMPS scans. The second purpose was to have a large enough quantity of dilute smoke for multiple SMPS scans. A 55 gallon drum was chosen for this purpose and the SAME smoke-in-drums setup was developed to enable SMPS measurements on a portion of the smoke output from the SAME piston chamber. Drum Hardware and Experimental Process The two 55 gallon drums were minimally modified for use in the experiment as follows: A muffin fan was bolted to the circular drum floor opposite the removable lid. All other modifications were made to the lid, including feed￾through adapters for tubing and the electrical fan cord, and mounted HEPA filters through which clean air was provided for purging. A four-way crossover valve enabled the drum to be either filled with smoke via a vacuum pump preceded by a flow-controlling orifice, or bypassed by the smoke, which effectively isolated the SAME hardware from high pressure during the drum purging process. Transfer of un-aged smoke into the drum began when the SAME software commanded the valve opening and lowered the piston in the aging chamber causing half of the chamber volume to be expelled (3 liter

n the SAME software commanded the valve opening and lowered the piston in the aging chamber causing half of the chamber volume to be expelled (3 liters), with the remainder of the smoke retained in the chamber and allowed to age for 12 minutes. The flow rate into the drum was 1.7 L/min, matching the flow rate of the DustTrak™ instrument that the drums replaced. It took less than 2 minutes to transfer the smoke sample into the drum. Tubing from the SAME hardware to the drums was less than one meter in order to minimize transport losses of smoke particles. Initial calculations from previous SAME data indicated that for all materials, the aerosol concentration in the drum would be less than 2 × 104 particles/cm3 , which is below the rule-of-thumb threshold concentration of 106 particles/cm3 . Below this level, coagulation can be neglected since it will occur at a very slow rate.15 Thus it could be assumed that very little aging took place in the drum during the SMPS measurements of un-aged smoke. During each SMPS sample, the volume of air removed was between 0.5 % and 1.5 % of the drum volume and a correspondingly small number of particles were removed so the drum aerosol concentration was relatively constant during the measurements. Any make-up air needed during the sampling was drawn in through the HEPA filters on the drum lid. The fan in the drum was used to mix the smoke and prevent stratification which could skew the SMPS measurements. First, a 10:1 sheath-to-aerosol flow ratio was used for three consecutive measurements with high fidelity giving particle sizes up to 660 nm. Three subsequent samples were taken with a flow rate ratio of 5:1, in order to reach the largest measurable SMPS particle size of 1000 nm. Considering that aging increases particle size, the higher flow rate ratio (smaller range) gives results for only a portion of the true aged size distribution for most materials in this experiment. Log-probability Plot The log-probability plot is a graphical technique used to assess lognormality of an aerosol. Discrete data from the SMPS size bins and TEM size distributions are plotted on the probability scale. Lognormal distributions will be a straight line, and volume and number size distributions should be parallel, indicating that σg is the same for both distributions but with different means. Extremes on the graphs can be neglected in the log probability plots for number distributions when they deviate from the straight line fit for 5% or less of the extremes of the probability scale (Hinds, 1999). For the SMPS data, these deviations are the result of poor counting statistics in the large diameter tail and lack of measurement range (for lamp wick and silicone), which particularly affects the volume distribution plots. ore complicated. First of all, it was realized that the orifice that controls the diluting N2 flow was not working under the critical flow regime as original designed. From the logged data in the engineering data file, the N2 pressure upstream the orifice, which is a regulated pressure, is not high enough to maintain a critical flow. This pressure varied much more than it was supposed to, indicating that the regulator is undersized. Thus, the actual diluting N2 flow rate depends on both upstream and downstream pressure of the orifice and the size of the orifice and the temperature as well, although the temperature dependency is weak. The total flow rate going through a DustTrak is controlled by the orifice in each CDE, which is truly working under critical flow regime. Thus for the two DustTraks in the SAME apparatus, there are totally 4 orifices, two for the diluting N2 flows installed in the fluid control unit and two for the total flows installed with each DustTrak in its CDE. s. When studying effects of gravity on the smoke properties, we want to compare smokes generated at the same temperature. For SAME and SAMER, during a test, the software controls the temperature via the resistance of heating wire. It is true that for the same wire coil, constant wire resistance means constant wire temperature. Traditionally, test conditions are specified by Rt/R0, the ratio between the resistance of heated wire over the resistance of the wire at room temperature. Thus, before each run, the sample wire resistance is measured, then multiplied by this parameter to get the target resistance for the control circuitry. Although, Rt/R0 can uniquely define the temperature, it is not clear what actual sample temperature is. Since the wire resistance is one of the parameters that are logged in the engineering data sheet which makes it possible to derive actual temperature from the logged resistances. However, when deriving wire temperatures, one has to take the fact into account that the wire length varies from sample to sample and so called room temperature varies too. After

After the heating temperatures were obtained, it is surprising that for the same Rt/R0, the actual heating temperature difference can be as large as 30 degrees Celsius. The following is how this is carried out. SAME heater temperature modeling.

Objective: It was identified that each sample has a significant length of leading section of the resistive wire. This section does not touch the sample material and is exposed in air flow. Thus the temperature of this leading section is different from the portion of the wire that contacts the sample material. The control circuitry only controls the total resistance of the heating wire, not individual portion of the wire. Our goal is to find the temperature of the wire that is in contact with the sample material. Formulation: Hypothesis: the temperature difference between the two portions of the wire is caused by different convection heat transfer from the two. The wire that is in contact with the sample has less heat loss from the convection heat transfer because about half of its surface area is covered by the sample material. Assumptions and simplifications: 1) Assume the entire wire consists of two distinct portions, one is in air (portion 1) and the other (portion 2) is in touch with the sample so that only half of the wire area is exposed to air. 2) Uniform cross section area of

ortion 1) and the other (portion 2) is in touch with the sample so that only half of the wire area is exposed to air. 2) Uniform cross section area of the wire, so the resistance is proportional to the length and the resistivity of the wire. 3) Resistivity is a known function of temperature. 4) Temperature distribution inside wire is uniform. 5) Newton convective heat transfer equation applies to both sections but with different coefficients. Although the port 2 is half exposed in air where convective equation works and half in contact with sample where transient conduction heat transfer should be used, for the sake of simplicity, we lump the two mechanisms together and use convection only with a modified heat transfer coefficient. or limited particle size range Theoretically, a lognormal distribution is defined in the particle size from zero to infinity, whereas any instrument used to measure certain moment of an aerosol inevitably has a limited particle size range. In some cases, an impacter is inserted in the inlet of an instrument to eliminate particles larger than certain size. In these cases, the instrument cannot sense the entire range of the distribution as the theory describes. Thus, one would like to know how much signal is lost due to the limited effective particle size range, or what the percentage of the total signal the instrument receives. This piece of information is useful to assess errors induced by omitting particles in a certain size range. It was found this question can be answered conveniently using the error function calculations, which is available in the Excel spread sheet or some other computational software or even in the tables of most mathematical handbooks. The reflight experiment built upon the results of the original flight during Expedition 15 by adding diagnostic measurements and expanding the test matrix. Five different materials representative of those found in spacecraft (Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell) were heated to temperatures below the ignition point with conditions controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air fl

The air flow past the sample during the heating period ranged from quiescent to 8 cm/s. The smoke was initially collected in an aging chamber to simulate the transport time from the smoke source to the detector. This effective transport time was varied by holding the smoke in the aging chamber for times ranging from 11 to 1800 s. Smoke particle samples were collected on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The TEM grids were analyzed to observe the particle morphology and size parameters. The diagnostics included a prototype two-moment smoke detector and three different measures of moments of the particle size distribution. These moment diagnostics were used to determine the particle number concentration (zeroth moment), the diameter concentration (first moment), and the mass concentration (third moment). st moment), and the mass concentration (third moment). I. Introduction ppropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters. Terrestrial fire detection systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.1, 2 Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial designs. There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.3 Microgravity fires have been found to have radically different structure from their normal-gravity (a.k.a. 1-g) counterparts. The limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of early detection. Finally the materials used in spacecraft are different from typical terrestrial applications where s

fire increase the importance of early detection. Finally the materials used in spacecraft are different from typical terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size distribution. The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors. Smoke Background Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In particular it can include unburned, recondensed, original polymer or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid, hydrocarbon soot, condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth. Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequent

trained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot. Prior spacecraft systems are summarized in more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban.4, 5 In the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were limited and mission durations were short, consequently it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors.4 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms. The Space Shuttle Detectors were based upon ionization fire detector technology, the most advanced technology available at the time and used an inertial separator designed to eliminate particles larger than 1-2 micrometers. The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detectors use near-IR forward scattering, rendering them most sensitive to particles larger than a micrometer, outside of t

Space Station (ISS) smoke detectors use near-IR forward scattering, rendering them most sensitive to particles larger than a micrometer, outside of the range of sensitivity of the shuttle detector. As described by Friedman4 there have been six overheat and failed component events in the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several similar incidents that have occurred on the ISS. None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that failure of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences. As a result, improved understanding of spacecraft fire detection is critically needed.6 Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al.5 found that the particulate produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravity. Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment5 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smok

(Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment5 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient data concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft. II. SAME Experiment To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, another experiment was developed: the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aer

ng the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and some systems require substantial sample return to Earth. As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of the size distribution. When combined, these moments provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution. The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled in the SAME experiment. The experiment flew A

twice the first time in 2007 (SAME-1) and the second (SAME-2) in 2010. When discussion applies to both flights, this paper will refer to “SAME.” If the discussion is specific to a particular flight, the flight number will be identified e.g. “SAME-2.” E. The average particle size and an estimate of the width of the size distribution will be estimated from various moments of the size distribution. Calibration was accomplished using two different aerosol generators one using mono￾disperse particle generation using dioctyl phthalate (DOP) according to the approach by Mulholland and Liu11 and the other using polystyrene spheres. For SAME-2, one of the DustTrak devices was replaced by a new device the MPASS (Multi-Parameter Aerosol Scattering Sensor) which is an optical scattering sensor, employing two detectors placed at fixed angles. G. Experimental Results Over 100 sample materials were tested. These were comprised of samples of 6 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, Pyrell™, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. The test conditions included multiple sample temperatures and air flow rates. The baseline air flow rate was 8 cm/s with runs conducted at rates down to 2 cm/s with a limited set conducted with no airflow while the sample was heated. The sample temperatures were based on the pyrolysis properties of the material and were thus material specific. The baseline temperature was selected to produce 1 to 2 mg of weight loss in 60 seconds and have reasonable signal on each of the moment instruments. To examine the effect of sample temperature, additional higher temperature conditions were also selected that would not saturate the moment instruments. The TEM girds recovered from the thermal precipitators on SAME-1 were unfortunately contaminated with extraneous particles whose origin is currently under investigation. For SAME-2 more rigorous assembly controls were follo

ortunately contaminated with extraneous particles whose origin is currently under investigation. For SAME-2 more rigorous assembly controls were followed and numerous good particle images were obtained. For typical runs, the particle concentrations were a few million particles / cc and the mass concentrations were 2 to 15 mg/m3 however there were runs with fewer particles. For these conditions, the typical numbers of particles sampled by the instruments were in the billions although for the test with the lowest particle concentrations the sample sizes were of the order of several million particles. 1. 2. MPASS Results The MPASS was included in SAME-2 to demonstrate the effectiveness of a two-moment smoke detector. Because of how they are used, a smoke detector is not calibrated for specific materials and instead has a single calibration for all conditions. The objective is to maintain a flat sensor response, regardless of the type of smoke or the particle size so the signal is proportional only to a selected moment (e.g. mass or number concentration). The approach used was to derive correlations to predict the smoke number concentration and mass concentration from the MPASS output. This correlation was made using the other SAME measurements (number and mass concentration) as a reference. A least-squares, third-order, correlation was computed on all test points with a signal to noise ratio greater than 2 independent of all other parameters (e.g. material, heating rate, and aging time). The results are shown in figures 9 and 10, for prediction of the mass concentration and the number concentration, respectively. Ideally these response graphs should be horizontal lines. Both figures show that the correlation decreases the relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor. 3. TEM Results Overall, 72 particle samples were taken on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids using the thermal precipitator. These samples were imaged with a TEM to evaluate the particle morphology as a function of flow conditions, material and heating level. Overall, silicone rubber and DBP presented no particles that were visible via TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged in the TEM. As seen in Table 1, aging did increase the average particle size, however this level of change is not readily visible in the TEM images, instead the most visible change is the disappearance of the smallest particles. . Particularly for the semi-liquid particles, this absorption of the smallest particles into larger particles is expected to have little or no apparent effect on the size of the larger particles because the diameter is the cube root of the volume. In the case of non-liquid particles, the smallest particles will nevertheless be unlikely to be visible via TEM when they are attached to larger particles. 4. Impact of flow on particle morphology As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are released via pyrolysis. These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the reaction with oxygen. As the gases move from the wire, the temperature and species concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and convection. With the decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage and nucleation of smoke particles will occur. These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the condensation of the pyrolysis gases. The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the order of ms or less. Over a longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian motion collide and stick together in a process known as coagulation. This process may continue for time scales of up to 103 s. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11). If the particles ar

particles will coalesce and form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11). If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an agglomerate structure composed of many primary particles connected in a low density fractal￾like structure. This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11). Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low-gravity condition, the convective flow past the heated wire, the wire temperature, and the aging time. As the wire temperature increases, more of the sample will be pyrolyzed and these gases will subsequently condense on the nuclei leading to a larger mass concentration of the aerosol and a larger diameter of average mass. An increase in the convective flow for a fixed wire temperature is expected to result in an increase in the pyrolysis rate and thus an increase in the mass concentration of the aerosol. Some results follow this trend with silicone rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increasing slightly with flow while Tef

A possible explanation is that holding the wire temperature fixed does not necessarily mean that the sample surface temperature distribution is precisely the same at different air flow speeds. Although these are expected to be small variations, given the exponential dependence of the pyrolysis kinetics on temperature, changes in the heat transport environment could change the sample surface temperature between the wire coils. A case of special interest is the case of zero-flow. The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion. Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm. Assuming a cubical geometry this would correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in the 6000 cm3 piston. If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case. This is expected to lead to more coagulation and a larger particle size. It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests. The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined for 11 tests by modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware. This resulted in a very high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortun

very high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume. As a result the total particle counts were lower than normal and the TEM grids had few particles. It is important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios. If one performed the same experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone. So the larger particle diameters observed in these zero-flow conditions are important to consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles. For the zero-flow case, the heat is transported primarily by conduction rather than convection. This is likely to result in a significant increase in the gas temperature relative to the case with 8 cm/s air flow. A striking effect of this temperature change is the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters w

se with 8 cm/s air flow. A striking effect of this temperature change is the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition (Fig 13). The results from the SAME experiment indicate that substantial differences in the size distributions of the smoke particles are evident for the five spacecraft materials that were tested. For the conditions of the SAME experiment, all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an ionization smoke detector. However, the aging results suggest that some materials such as silicone rubber can produce smoke that can reach sizes better detected by light scattering techniques. The zero flow conditions produced smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate. Since spacecraft fire conditions include an even wider array of materials than those tested here and a broader range of flow and temperature conditions, broad smoke aerosol size distributions can be expected from credible pre-fire overheat events. These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejection than single moment detec

s that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejection than single moment detectors. The results from the prototype 2-moment detector (MPASS) were very encouraging in this respect with the technique showing real potential as a means to respond to a broad particle range while avoiding excessive false alarms from nuisance sources. The TEM result demonstrated that fire particulate can be expected to have a broad range of morphologies influenced by heating rate, material and flow conditions. IV. iii Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) Abstract Leaks, fires, and spills are some of the most significant hazards that must be accounted for in the design of the environmental control and life-support system on spacecraft. While prevention is certainly the first line of defense against a fire, early detection of a overheat event or an actual fire allows the crew to respond before the hazard gets out of control. The limited options available for response to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications. This report describes the outcomes of the Smoke Aerosol Measurements Experiment (SAME), an experiment conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS) to characterize the size distribution of smoke particulate produced in low-gravity from a variety of overheated spacecraft materials The absence of gravity can impact not only the formation of the smoke particulate but also the aging and coagulation processes that occur as the particu

e absence of gravity can impact not only the formation of the smoke particulate but also the aging and coagulation processes that occur as the particulate are transported from their source to a detector. Based on the results of an earlier flight project carried out in the Glovebox of the Space Shuttle, (Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)), the soot particles generated and observed in low gravity environment tend to be larger in size than those in earth conditions. However, the preliminary results of CSD project were not conclusive because of a minor variation of the temperature of hot wire which heated the test sample to generate smoke, and also because the CSD apparatus could not measure the liquid drops existing in the smoke produced by several of the samples. Furthermore, the CSD project was not designed to provide on-orbit measurement of the particle size distribution. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment was designed to obtain this data that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration missions. Unfortunately, because of the relative

this data that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration missions. Unfortunately, because of the relatively small volume of the MSG, it cannot accommodate the instruments normally used in a ground-based laboratory to measure the size distribution of smoke particulate. Therefore, a new procedure was developed, the moment method, from which the characteristics of the particle size distribution can be inferred using a minimum number of portable instrument. The SAME experiments were conducted during Expedition 15 on the ISS. Four materials, typical of those found in spacecraft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, silicone rubber, and Teflon. A fifth material, dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) retained in a cotton wick was used as a reference. In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event, samples were heated to temperatures below the ignition point. The smoke generation conditions were controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The transport time from the smoke sour

eneration conditions were controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The transport time from the smoke source to the detector was simulated by holding the smoke in an aging chamber for times ranging from 10 seconds to 1800 seconds. Smoke particle samples were collected on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The smoke properties were measured using particulate aerosol diagnostics that measure different moments of the size distribution. These statistics were combined to determine the geometric mean particle sizes and geometric standard deviation, which is sufficient to describe the entire smoke distribution if a lognormal distribution is assumed. For comparison, smoke detectors from

iv the ISS and the space shuttle were also included in the SAME apparatus. The experimental results show that, for the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter. The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity. The knowledge gained from SAME can be used to establish design requirements for smoke detectors used in future spacecraft.

1 1. Introduction Appropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters. Terrestrial fire detection systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.1, 2 Unfortunately, there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently current spacecraft fire detectors were developed based upon experience on normal gravity fire behavior and properties. This approach was necessary given the absence of data concerning microgravity smoke particulate. However planned spacecraft and their planned missions outside of low earth-orbit will require increased reliability of fire detection systems in addition to robust false alarm resistance. Extended lunar-surface missions will require systems that are not influenced by lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources. The absence of buoyant flow increases the residence time in microgravity fires causing substantial changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire behavior seen in reduce

eases the residence time in microgravity fires causing substantial changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire behavior seen in reduced gravity, it is reasonable to expect that the signatures and detection requirements of these fires will change. There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.3 The materials used in spacecraft are different from those typically used in terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. More importantly, the limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size distribution. The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to

Smoke Background Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In particular for non-flaming combustion, the aerosol includes recondensed original material or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid. For flaming combustion, the aerosol includes soot particulate, condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth. Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot. The background regarding fire detection in US spacecraft is summarized

, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot. The background regarding fire detection in US spacecraft is summarized in this paper but is discussed in more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban4, 5 In the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were limited and mission durations were short, consequently it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors.4 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms. Details of the ISS and STS detector requirements are described by Steisslinger et al.6 A brief overview of the requirements is given below.

2 Space Shuttle Detectors: At the time the Space Shuttle Orbiter (Space Transportation System (STS)) was developed, smoke detection for terrestrial applications was becoming commonplace.1 In particular, ionization detectors were readily available but photoelectric (scattering or obscuration detectors) were generally unavailable due to the difficulty of producing stable light sources. There were no data available concerning the smoke or dust particle size distribution in low-gravity and the database for normal-gravity smoke characteristics was a fraction of what is available today. Consequently, the STS smoke detector (Fig. 1) employed a variant of the accepted ground-based approach (ionization detectors). The Orbiter has nine particle-ionization smoke detectors in avionics cooling air return lines in the mid￾deck and flight deck and the SpaceLab had six additional particle-ionization smoke detectors in the avionics lines.7 While the design rationale is not completely known, Celesco™ (later Brunswick Defense™) based their design on data that suggested incipient fires could be discrimi

ign rationale is not completely known, Celesco™ (later Brunswick Defense™) based their design on data that suggested incipient fires could be discriminated by looking for particulate in the 0.4 μm to 0.7 μm range.8 The use of a pump provided the opportunity to use a particle separator that rejected particulate larger than 1μm. This air pump increased the power requirements and reduced the operational life of the detector. The STS detector as built was designed to alarm at a particle loading of 2 mg/m3 for 5 seconds (based on 1 micron particles) or a 0.022 mg/m3 /s rise in concentration for 20 seconds9 . This provided the opportunity to produce a detector that required substantially less power, (1.5 Watts versus 9 Watts for the orbiter detector)6 and, with no moving parts, was quieter with a much longer operational life. SAME Experiment To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) was developed. The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically too large to be compatible with spacecraft experiment constraints. Thus, to obtain particulate size statistics with existing aerosol instrumentation would require the return of numerous samples to Earth. As will be describe

to obtain particulate size statistics with existing aerosol instrumentation would require the return of numerous samples to Earth. As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of the size distribution. When combined, these moments provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution if a lognormal distribution is assumed. The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled. A. The Moment Method The approach used by the SAME experiment is termed the ‘moment method’ for convenience.13 This approach consists of measuring three moments of the size distribution (the zeroth, first and third moment) on orbit, using several small, light-weight instruments. By applying the properties of the lognormal distribution to the measured moments, the total number concentration, Nt, the geometric mean diameter, Dg, and the geometric sta

ties of the lognormal distribution to the measured moments, the total number concentration, Nt, the geometric mean diameter, Dg, and the geometric standard deviation, g, of the aerosol can be estimated. Once these three parameters are known, the size distribution of the measured aerosol is uniquely defined, assuming that the distribution is lognormal. In what follows, we will explain how the moment method works. A.1. Principle of the moment method The number (or count) distribution of an aerosol describes the number of particles that fall into a certain size range in a unit volume of aerosol. The number distribution is sometimes also called size distribution. Mathematically, a distribution function can be expressed in four different, but related, forms. First, a distribution function can be expressed as a frequency (or density) distribution function or a cumulative distribution function. Then, each of the two can be expressed in terms of its normalized form or non-

Instrumentation The moment measurements were made using an assembly of three separate instruments. Two are industrial hygiene instruments manufactured by TSI and one is a modified residential smoke detector. The zeroth-moment instrument is a condensation nuclei counter, the P-Trak™ (TSI Inc.). This device operates by passing the aerosol-laden air stream through a region saturated with isopropanol vapor and then into a cooler region where the vapor condenses onto the particl

he aerosol-laden air stream through a region saturated with isopropanol vapor and then into a cooler region where the vapor condenses onto the particles increasing their diameter such that they can be readily counted by a light scattering device. This instrument is very robust and operates over a range of 0 to 105 particles/cm3 and 20 nm to 1 μm diameter. Some dilution is required since the smoke concentration in SAME ranges from about 0.5 × 106 to 5 × 106 particles/cm3 . There was also a concern that the isopropanol condensate would not return to the wick in low-gravity.5 To mitigate this

10 issue, the condensing section of the device was modified with very small grooves to improve conductance of the condensate back to the wick. These changes were tested in a separate space experiment with good results indicating the modified device could be used successfully in low gravity.5 The first-moment instrument is the ionization chamber taken from a residential smoke detector. This device uses an alpha-particle emitter to generate ions in a region within a DC electric field. Normally, the ions drift toward an electrode inside the ionization chamber producing a current. When particulate are present, the ions attach themselves to the particles thereby charging the particles. Because the charged particles have a much smaller mobility than ions alone, the current is reduced. The required particle concentrations are on the order of 105 particles/cm3 , thus no sample dilution was required. The third-moment instrument is a light scattering device, the DustTrak™ (TSI Inc.). The device uses a 90 degree light scattering signal to quantify the aerosol mass density. For terrestrial dust

ring device, the DustTrak™ (TSI Inc.). The device uses a 90 degree light scattering signal to quantify the aerosol mass density. The device operating range is from 0.001 mg/m3 to 100 mg /m3 . These devices are equipped with an aerodynamic impactor at the inlet which captures particles larger than the selected size. The SAME experiment included 2 DustTraks™, one with a 1 μm impactor and the other with a 10 μm impactor. The difference in the signal from the two devices provided a measure of the fraction of the particulate that was larger than 1 μm. Realizing that crew time was the most precious ISS resource, SAME was designed to be operated both autonomously and from the ground to the greatest extent possible. The SAME hardware was organized into a number of smaller modular units to facilitate stowage for launch, provide for easy change out, increase the reliability and reduce risk. The downside of this strategy was that the assembly of the experiment involved many connections and required approximately 5 hours of crew time. Once installed, however, SAME was easily and effectively operated from the Tele Science Center (TSC) at the Glenn Research Center (GRC), and this capability enabled the ground team to achieve roughly a 50% greater number of test points (and data) than was originally planned. These low populations of larger particles are consistent with the less effective detection by light scattering devices which was seen for some of the Teflon tests and with the signals obtained from the STS and ISS detectors. Closing Remarks The SAME project successfully implemented the moment method described in this report, under the volume constraints of the ISS MSG, to determine the size distribution of the smokes generated from 5 tested materials in well controlled conditions of heating temperature, heating time and air flow rate. In combination with the knowledge gained from previous CSD experiment, it becomes obvious that the detection of smoke across the size range seen in SAME and CSD, while still discriminating against dust (which tends to be large), will probably require a detection system that can discriminate the particle size distribution to at least a limited degree. Two possible effective means of achieving this size discrimination are to employ a detector that measures more than one moment of the size distributio

Yang National Institute of Standards and Technology Zengguang Yuan, Victoria Bryg National Center for Space Exploration Research Copyright © 2009 SAE International ABSTRACT This paper presents results from a smoke detection experiment entitled Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) which was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the International Space Station (ISS) during Expedition 15. Five different materials representative of those found in spacecraft were pyrolyzed at temperatures below the ignition point with conditions controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The sample materials were Teflon®, Kapton®, cellulose, silicone rubber and dibutylphthalate. The transport time from the smoke source to the detector was simulated by holding the smoke in an aging chamber for times ranging from 10 to1800 seconds. Smoke particle samples were collected on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The smoke particle size distributions were measured using three particulate aerosol diagnostics that measure different moments of the size distribution and smoke detectors from the ISS and the space shuttle. These diagnostics were used to estimate the particle number concentration (zeroth moment), the diameter concentration (first moment) and the mass concentration (third moment). These values were combined to estimate the diameter of average mass, the count mean diameter, the geometric mean diameter and the geometric standard deviation. Even though the analysis of these data is ongoing, information from the various instruments and the calculated mean particle sizes has important implications for the design of spacecraft smoke detectors. INTRODUCTION Design of fire detector systems requires understanding of the background conditions and the expected range of events to be detected. Detectors for terrestrial fires were developed using the results of extensive study of terrestrial fires.1,2 Unfortunately, there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently current spacecraft fire detectors were developed based upon experience from terrestrial systems. Given the large changes in fire behavior seen in reduced gravity, it is reasonable to expect that the smoke characteristics and detection requirements of these fires will change. The absence of buoyant flow in B-1 Appendix B

low-gravity increases the residence time in microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.3 The materials used in spacecraft are different from typical terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. Very significantly, the limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications. All of these effects can be expected to change the detection requirements: both the smoke concentration sensitivity, and the expected smoke particle size distribution. The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors. SMOKE BACKGROUND Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In particular it can include unburned, recondensed, original polymer or pyrolysis products that can be liquid, solid, carbonaceous soot, condensed water vapor, or ash particles. Soot particles domi

sed, original polymer or pyrolysis products that can be liquid, solid, carbonaceous soot, condensed water vapor, or ash particles. Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth. Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot. Prior spacecraft systems are summarized in more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban.4,5 In the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were limited and mission durations were short. Consequently it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors.4 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms. The Space Shuttle (Space Tra

ng fire detectors.4 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms. The Space Shuttle (Space Transportation System (STS)) detectors were based upon ionization fire detector technology, the most advanced technology available at the time and used an inertial separator designed to eliminate particles larger than 1-2 micrometers. The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detectors use near-IR forward scattering, rendering them most sensitive to particles larger than a micrometer, outside of the range of sensitivity of the shuttle detector. More details of the ISS and STS detector requirements are presented by Steisslinger et al. 6 however the basic details are summarized below. The STS detector, as built, was designed to alarm at 2 mg/m3 (based on 1 micrometer particles) or 0.022 mg/m3 /s rise in concentration for 20 seconds. The ISS detector was designed to alarm at obscuration of 1% per foot using an Underwriters Laboratory (UL) smoke box and a white light extinction meter. This was implemented using a transfer standard detector a

per foot using an Underwriters Laboratory (UL) smoke box and a white light extinction meter. This was implemented using a transfer standard detector and a 0.5 micrometer polystyrene latex-bead aerosol system that was used to set the amplifiers on each unit. The transfer standard was calibrated in the smoke box and then used to set the levels with the aerosol system. As described by Friedman4 there have been six overheat and failed component failures in the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several similar incidents that have occurred on the ISS. None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that failure of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences. As a result, improved understanding of spacecraft fire detection is critically needed.7 Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al. 5 found that the particulate produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravit

found that the particulate produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravity. Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment5 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient data concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft. SAME EXPERIMENT CONCEPT To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, another experiment, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), was developed. The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by t

another experiment, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), was developed. The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and may require substantial sample return to Earth. As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to estimate separate moments of the size distribution. When combined, these moments provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution. The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment, however, the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled. INSTRUMENTS More details of the experiment hardware and its calibration are presented elsewhere,11,12 however a brief summary follows. The moment measurements were made using an assembly of three separate instruments. Two are industrial hygiene instruments manufactured by TSI and one is a modified residential smoke detector. The zeroth-moment instrument is a condensation nuclei counter P-Trak® (TSI Inc.). This device operates by passing the aerosol-laden particle stream through a region saturated with isopropanol vapor and then into a cooler region where the vapor condenses onto the particles increasing their diameter such that they can be readily counted by a light scattering detector. This instrument is very robust and operates over a range of 0 to 105 particles/cm3 and 20 nm to 4 to 5 μm diameter. Some dilution is required, since the allowable smoke concentration ranges from about 0.5 × 106 to 5 × 106 particles / cm3 . The first-moment instrument is an ionization chamber from a residential smoke detector. This device uses an alpha-particle emitter (Am241) to generate ions in a reg

nt instrument is an ionization chamber from a residential smoke detector. This device uses an alpha-particle emitter (Am241) to generate ions in a region within a DC electric field. The drift of the ions in the electric field results in a current. The presence of particulate reduces the current as a result of the attachment of the ions to the particulate. The mobility of the charged aerosol is too small for it to be collected on the ionization chamber electrode. The required particle concentrations are on the order of 105 particles/cm3 , and no sample dilution was required. The third-moment instrument is a light scattering device DustTrak® (TSI Inc.). The device measures the intensity of light scattered by the smoke aerosol at a scattering angle of about 90 degrees light scattering signal to quantify the aerosol mass. This light scattering signal is approximately proportional to the mass concentration; however, to compensate for the non￾linearity of the relationship between mass and the scattering signal density, additional analysis based on Mie Scattering theory or calibration with

￾linearity of the relationship between mass and the scattering signal density, additional analysis based on Mie Scattering theory or calibration with the specific aerosol material is required. The device’s operating range is from 0.001 mg/m3 to 100 mg/m3 . These devices are equipped with an aerodynamic impactor at the inlet which captures particles larger than the selected size. The SAME experiment included 2 DustTraks® one with a 1 μm impactor and one with a 10 μm impactor. The difference in the signal from these two devices provided a measure of the fraction of the particulate that was larger than 1 μm. In some cases dilution was required owing to the high smoke concentration levels. A schematic of the assembled hardware appears in Fig. 2. The system was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox, an ISS facility that provides many resources including: containment, power, data, video and uplink commanding. Smoke was generated by overheating a small sample of material in the smoke generation duct for approximately 60 seconds. During this interval, controlled flow was induced by

verheating a small sample of material in the smoke generation duct for approximately 60 seconds. During this interval, controlled flow was induced by a moving piston in the aging chamber which drew the smoke into the chamber. The smoke was held in the aging chamber for a predetermined time, allowing the particles to coagulate. After a specified aging time, the smoke was then pushed by the piston into the diagnostics duct where the moment instruments made their measurements. Also installed in the diagnostics duct were space shuttle and ISS smoke detectors. As the smoke was monitored by the moment instruments, a sample of the smoke particles was deposited on a Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grid via a thermal precipitator which uses thermophoresis to deposit the particles on the grids. The zeroth and first moment devices showed good linearity over the conditions of interest however, the third moment device (TSI- DustTrak®) is theoretically predicted to show non-monotonic behavior as particle size is increased. While a satisfactory prediction of the DustTrak® response was obtain

retically predicted to show non-monotonic behavior as particle size is increased. While a satisfactory prediction of the DustTrak® response was obtained using liquid droplets of dioctyl phthalate, the uncertainty associated with the Mie scattering calculations due to the particle refractive index estimate, the potential of agglomerated particles, and deviation from assumed log-normal size distribution must be assessed further for the smoke samples here. In the results reported here, the DustTrak® response was directly calibrated, for each smoke source, against mass concentration measurements using a tapered element oscillating microbalance. This approach is valid as long as the size distribution of the sample does not change significantly. Using estimated material densities, the diameter of average mass was computed for each sample. Equation 7 was used to compute the geometric standard deviation from the arithmetic mean diameter and the diameter of average mass, and Equation 6 was used to compute the GMD. Figure 2. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS Overall, 30 sample materials were tested. These were comprised of six samples each of 5 materials: Teflon®, Kapton®, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. Geometric Mean (GMD), Arithmetic Mean, and Average Mass diameters and the Geometric Standard Deviation (GSD) results from the moment instruments for baseline runs (no aging) and 720 second aging are presented in Table 1. Introduction ppropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters. Terrestrial fire detection systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.1, 2 Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial designs. There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.3 Microgravity fires have been found to have radically different structure from their 1-g counterparts. The limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fir

fires have been found to have radically different structure from their 1-g counterparts. The limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of early detection. Finally the materials used in spacecraft are different from typical terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size distribution. The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics 2 Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In particular it can include unburned, recondensed, original polymer or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid, hydrocarbon soot, condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth. Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot. Prior spacecraft systems are summarized in more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban.4, 5 In the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were limited and mission durations were short, consequently it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. SAME Experiment To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, another experiment the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) was developed. The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and may require substantial sample return to Earth. As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of the size distribution.
