Overview The CFI experiments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments onboard the ISS to further explore the newly discovered quasi-steady “cool flames.” Cool flames are controlled by low temperature chemistry, and occur in the NTC region of n-alkane fuels. FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of

able flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K. Since the cool-flame chemistry depends on the chemical structure of the fuel as well as pressure and temperature, three different fuel combinations were investigated, namely, pure n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso￾dodecane mixtures and farnesane ( a renewable jet fuel) at ambient pressures up to 5 atmospheres. Cool flame extinction occurs when its static stability is lost close to the lower turnover point in the NTC region, addition of helium to the ambient gas is also considered. Results for droplet burning rates, flame dynamics, droplet extinction diameters, and flame radiant out put are measured. 2. Introduction (PS): Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day which averages out to an astonish

nd fundamental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day which averages out to an astonishing 2.5 gallons per day per person (Reitz, 2013). The primary reasons for such a high reliance on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but globally, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability compared to many other forms of energy. With the emergence of newer internal combustion engine technologies such as Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) and Reactivity-Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) engines, understanding the autoignition and heat release chemistry and kinetics of hydrocarbon fuels is more important that ever. These new technologies coupled with the emergence of major sources of renewable fuels for both gasoline and diesel applications, including butanols and heavier alcohols, bio-diesel, farnesane and high carbon number synthetics, further emphasize the need to understand the kinetic effects of blending renewables with petroleum derived fuels. a. Objectives Cool flame phenomena are influenced by a number of factors, including the fuel molecular structure (for pure fuel cases), the ambient environment (pressure, temperature, oxygen and diluent (He) concentrations), and the fuel composition (the mixture of fuel structures and perhaps fuel additives such as those used to change octane or cetane behavior). Though it is not possible to examine all of these factors in a thorough manner, here we propose a set of experiments that explore each one of these factors, namely, fuel structure effects, ambient conditions effect, fuel mixture effects, and the presence of fuel additives.

Background Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 1

he combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day, which averages out to an amazing 2.5 gallons per day per person. The primary reason for such high reliance on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but in the rest of the world, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability, compared to many other forms of energy sources. With the emergence of newer technologies for internal combustion engines and the increasing use of renewable bio-fuels, such as the Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engine and bio-diesel, that promise cleaner more efficient and sustainable utilization of hydrocarbon fuels, the need to understand the fundamental chemical and physical aspects of liquid-fuel combustion is bound to increase. Commercially available transportation fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are comprised of many hydrocarbon compounds, normal alkanes and branched alkanes be

able transportation fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are comprised of many hydrocarbon compounds, normal alkanes and branched alkanes being major components. The combustion characteristics of these alkanes are quite complex and follow branched-chain reaction pathways involving many intermediate radicals. The chemical pathways vary, depending on temperature and, to a lesser extent, on pressure. In general it is possible to identify a low-temperature reaction mechanism and a high￾temperature mechanism, with a transition region between them. Many hydrocarbons exhibit a unique feature in this transition region, namely that the reaction rate decreases with increasing temperature,

4 leading it to be called the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) region. There area a number of models available in the literature, simplified chemical-kinetic model involving hundreds of reactions as well as detailed mechanisms involving thousands of reactions. Droplet-combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) conducted onboard the International Space Station, as part of the Flame Extinguishment Experiments, have revealed for the first time that large n-alkane droplets can continue to burn quasi-steadily in the NTC region (see, Fig 1). NTC behavior of the heat-release rate is necessary for low-temperature quasi-steady droplet burning to be stable. It was observed that the second￾stage combustion of the droplet controlled by low-temperature NTC chemistry, referred to as ``cool-flame combustion" here for the sake of simplicity, abruptly ends at a finite droplet diameter, leaving the unburned droplet to vaporize in the hot atmosphere. A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction. Figure 1. T

apor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction. Figure 1. Three representative examples of radiative extinction and subsequent cool flame combustion of n￾heptane droplets in air. Inset shows the visible flame, backlit droplet images and the vapor cloud formation. Furthermore, the second-stage flame is shown to lie closer to the droplet surface where the rates of heat generation by the NTC chemistry is dynamically balanced by the heat loss rate. Unlike the hot-flame combustion where the overall process is controlled by equilibrium thermodynamic properties of the fuel, the cool-flame combustion depends on the chemical-kinetic details of the NTC region. These experimental and numerical studies provide a new tool to further explore the NTC chemistry of liquid fuels in an entirely new way. The experimental cool-flame droplet burning rates provide measures of the heat-release rates and stoichiometry, the flame-diameter evolution provides insight into hot-flame diffusive and convective heat-loss effec

res of the heat-release rates and stoichiometry, the flame-diameter evolution provides insight into hot-flame diffusive and convective heat-loss effects, and the droplet extinction diameter provides a stringent measurement of chemical-kinetic characteristic times. The objectives of the CFI experiments is to further explore the cool flame phenomenon using pure fuels, and fuel mixtures over a range of pressures and helium dilution. b. Rational for Microgravity (if unusual)

5 Rationale for microgravity remains the same for all the droplet combustion experiments conducted onboard the ISS. In microgravity the droplets burn in a spherically symmetric form, and therefore it is possible to model the processes with complex chemical kinetic mechanisms involving thousands of reactions leading to a better understanding of the chemistry. Moreover, the cool flames need much longer residence times and cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames. c. NRA the Investigation was Selected Under This project was initiated by NASA through a Science Definition Team (SDT) which formulated the overall objectives. It was peer reviewed by an independent panel of scientists and approved by NASA HQ as a follow-up experiments to FLEX, and FLEX-2 in the CIR using additional fuels and gases needed to complete the test matrix. The experimental hardware is same as that of the FLEX experiments with few minor modifications in the data acquisition systems. d. Operations a. Procedures The operational procedure used in the CFI tests is the same as for the FLEX experiments. Once the ISS crew installs the required fuel syringe, and the gas bottles containing the gas mixtures in the MDCA and CIR facilities, all the actual experimental operations are conducted from the ground at the Telescience Support Center (TSC) located at the NASA Glenn Research Center. Prior to each test the combustion chamber is filled with the specified gas mixture at the required pressure, and the hot-wire igniters are positioned close to the droplet deployment site. Subsequently, a droplet of desired size is dispensed between the hypodermic needles and freely deployed, and ignited. The igniter is withdrawn from the FOV once ignition is detected. he igniter is withdrawn from the FOV once ignition is detected. When required a 40 micron silicon-carbide fiber is used to tether the droplet at one place and stop it from drifting off from the field of view. The combustion process is recorded using a backlit, black-and-white camera ( 5 cm X 5 cm FOV) to obtain droplet size as a function of time, a UV-sensitive camera is used to image the OH* emission from the flame which provides the flame size data. A color camera which is had a live downlink to the TSC is used to perform and monitor the overall process. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers are used to measure the radiation emission from the flame. Details of the experimental hardware and the data reduction procedures can be found in Dietrich et al. (2014) b. On-Orbit Testing Over two hundred tests were carried out during the CFI experimental campaign. The initial droplet size was kept around 4 mm so that radiative extinction and the subsequent cool flame combustion can be observed. The list of experiments performed are as follows: • Pure n-dodecane at 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 2, 3, an

subsequent cool flame combustion can be observed. The list of experiments performed are as follows: • Pure n-dodecane at 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 2, 3, and 5 atm. • N-dodecane/Iso-dodecane mixtures: 75/25% and 60/40% by mass at pressures from 0.5 to 5 atm • Helium dilution by 29% and 59% with O2 mole fraction at 0.21 • Farnesane: from 0.75 to 3 atm c. Anomalies That Effect Science Surprises/New Discovery No new anomalies or surprises were observed during the CFI experiments. However, as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed. This behavior is unexpected based on earlier observations from FLEX experiments. Furthermore, the soot-shell

6 which surrounds the droplet and lies between the droplet surface and the flame, became unstable and ill￾defined at higher pressures, a phenomenon which is not fully understood. d. Results a. Findings All the CFI data is yet to be fully analyzed and interpreted using theoretical and numerical models. A brief overview of general observations made during preliminary data analysis prior to posting on the PSI website is presented below. Interested researchers are welcome to propose to NASA for further analysis and interpretation of CFI data. 5.1 Cool flames: Cool flames were observed during n-dodecanol combustion as well as n-dodecanol/iso-dodecanol mixture cases. The addition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol. Figure 1 shows a typical case of cool-flame behavior for n-dodecanol.

dition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol. Figure 1 shows a typical case of cool-flame behavior for n-dodecanol. Figure 1. FLEX-1223: N-dodecane at 1.25 atm pressure in air. 5.2 Warm flames: Warm flames are a consequence of changing in chemical pathway during n-alkane oxidation. Figure 2 shows (Westbrook, 2010) the various chemical pathways: cool flames occur when low-temperature branching is dominant, when intermediate temperatures become more active warm flames are established. During warm flames the heat release rate dynamically balance the heat loss rate. Addition of helium seems to enhance this balance within the NTC region.

7 Figure 2. Chemical kinetic pathways for n-alkane oxidation (Westbrook, 2010). Figure 3: FLEX-1268 – N-dodecane at 3 atm burning in 12%O2 – 50% N2 – 29% Helium. Reignition and warm flame formation are shown. Warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and the flame is not visible in the color camera. Subsequently, a hot flame is ignited which quickly extinguishes to form a cool flame. 5.3 Cool flame extinction:

8 Cool flame extinction is controlled primarily by chemical kinetics. As the droplet size decreases, the residence time in the reaction zone of the gas-phase diffusion flame is reduced to a value corresponding to which the cool flame becomes statically unstable, and this leads to cool flame extinction. Figure 4 shows the cool flame extinction diameter as function of ambient pressure for both free-floated and fiber-supported droplets for pure n-dodecane burning in air. As mentioned earlier, as the pressure is increased above approximately 2 atm, reignitions were commonly observed, eventually leading to complete combustion of the fuel droplet. It is interesting to note that the 40 micron fiber shows relatively little effect on the extinction diameter. Figure 4. Cool flame extinction diameters as a function of ambient pressure for n-dodecane droplets burning in air. Since the cool flame extinction is an instability phenomenon where the dynamic balance between heat release and heat loss from the flame is lost at the lower turning point in the NTC region, one would expect addition of heli

amic balance between heat release and heat loss from the flame is lost at the lower turning point in the NTC region, one would expect addition of helium to have a substantial influence on the process. Figure 5 illustrates the effect of helium dilution on the extinction diameter for n-dodecane. Increase helium dilution leads to earlier cool flame extinction giving a larger extinction diameter.

9 Figure 5. Effect of helium dilution on cool flame extinction during n-dodecane droplet combustion. 5.4 Sooting behavior as function of ambient pressure: The effects and the process of soot formation during cool flame combustion remains largely unexplored. The shoot shell that forms during hot flame is stabilized by the balance of force between fluid mechanical drag and the thermophoretic force. At low pressures a stable spherical soot-shell is formed. However, as the pressure increase the soot-shell becomes diffuse and undefined. The reasons for this phenomenon is still not well understood. At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet surface. But, when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot flame extinction. The mechanisms behind this process has not been fully understood, and further analysis and research is needed.

10 Figure 6. Backlit images of the droplet during hot and cool flame burning at atmospheric pressures of approximately 380, 570, 760, 1520, 2280 and 3800 mmHg. The hot flame images are approximately 4 sec after igniter withdraw and the cool flame images are approximately 5 sec after hot flame extinction. The droplet in the cool flame image at 1520 mmHg was close to the edge of the FOV. The red circles during hot flame burning at the two highest pressures show the approximate location of the droplet surface. 5.5 Summary of findings: CFI experiments has provided cool flame burning data for pure n-dodecane, and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures. Farnesane, a commercially available renewable fuel characteristics were also studied. The effect of pressure and helium dilution were studied for these fuels. Data for droplet regression rate, hot and cool flame diameters, extinction conditions, and radiant emission, both broad band and narrow band, are obtained and posted to the PSI website. b. Benefits Low temperature chemistry is of fundamental importance in the combustion of many practical fu

are obtained and posted to the PSI website. b. Benefits Low temperature chemistry is of fundamental importance in the combustion of many practical fuels. Low temperature chemistry controls the autoignition of fuels when injected into a combustion chamber, and in homogeneous mixtures of fuel and oxygen. New internal combustion engines, such as the HCCI engines, operate at low temperatures reducing the pollution formation and increasing overall efficiencies. The CFI experimental measurements provide a useful way to validate the complex chemical kinetic mechanisms that are being developed. The cool flame combustion process itself maybe of use in fuel reformulation technologies to produce hydrogen in fuel cell applications. c. Patents None 6. Glenn Research Center, 21000 Brookpark Road, Cleveland, OH 44135, Email: william.r.schoren@nasa.gov ABSTRACT Since 2012, the Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) has been under development by the Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (SFS Demo) project that is funded by NASA’s Advanced Exploration Systems Division in the Human Exploration and Operations Mission Directorate. The overall objective of this project is to reduce the uncertainty and risk associated with the design of spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA’s exploration missions. This is accomplished by defining, developing, and conducting experiments that address gaps in spacecraft fire safety knowledge and capabilities identified by NASA’s Fire Safety System Maturation Team. This paper describes the three Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire-I, -II, and -III) that were developed at NASA-GRC and that will conduct a series of material flammability tests in low-gravity and at length s

text: Saffire-I, -II, and -III) that were developed at NASA-GRC and that will conduct a series of material flammability tests in low-gravity and at length scales that are realistic for a spacecraft fire. The experiments will be conducted in Orbital ATK’s Cygnus vehicle after it has unberthed from the International Space Station. The tests will be fully automated with the data downlinked at the conclusion of the test and before the Cygnus vehicle reenters the atmosphere. INTRODUCTION Tests on full-scale transportation vehicles, buildings, homes, and habitats have been common on earth to more fully understand the fire hazards associated with each application and how best to protect the passengers and inhabitants from a potential fire. Fire safety on spacecraft has been a significant concern for NASA during the decades of crewed spaceflight and will remain so as NASA plans future exploration missions. Many microgravity combustion experiments have been performed on the Space Shuttle and continue to be performed on the International Space States (ISS) and the data from these experiments have contributed to our understanding of how to prevent and protect crewed spacecraft from fire. However, none of these experiments have studied sample and environment sizes typical of those expected in a spacecraft fire [

text: ed spacecraft from fire. However, none of these experiments have studied sample and environment sizes typical of those expected in a spacecraft fire [1]. Prior experiments have been limited to samples no larger than 10 cm in length and width whereas a serious spacecraft fire would likely be much larger and consume much more material. Because of the large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, there is a significant lack of data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. The use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. Despite their obvious importance, full scale spacecraft fire experiments have not been possible because of the inherent hazards involved with conducting a large fire test

The major safety hazard is inadvertent igniter activation prior to the Cygnus de￾berthing from the ISS. This would result in the exposure of the flight crew to toxic gases that are produced from the combustion event. It should be noted that this hazard is a concern prior to Cygnus berthing to the ISS since the toxic gases would be present when the Cygnus hatch is opened to the ISS. The power and communication interfaces between Cygnus and Saffire are utilized to control this hazard. Cygnus provides two power feed circuits to Saffire due to power requirements. One power feed circuit provides power to the Saffire avionics, the other provides power to the igniter circuitry. There are two latching relays in each of these two power feed circuits, one in the power feed side, one in the return. These four latching relays are contained within the Saffire flight unit but are controlled and monitored by Cygnus avionics. A separate ground comma

text: . These four latching relays are contained within the Saffire flight unit but are controlled and monitored by Cygnus avionics. A separate ground command to the Cygnus avionics is required to close each of these four latching relays. Igniter activation requires that all four relays be closed. This is because Saffire avionics provides an enable command to a DC/DC converter in the igniter circuitry and also provides commanding to solid state relay switches on the igniter control card within the igniter power feed circuitry. In addition, a ground command to the Saffire avionics via Cygnus avionics is required to initiate an igniter activation for an experiment run. Cygnus avionics and the associated ground commanding provide the required failure tolerance for control of the Saffire hazard of inadvertent igniter activation. One of the drawbacks of these experiments is that a relatively small number of tests will be conducted (two large samples and nine smaller samples). A thorough evaluation of these phenomena would require many more samples and range of materials. Also, if they are typical of most low-g combustion experiments, the findings will raise additional significant questions for material flammability in spacecraft. The Saffire hardware and the Cygnus vehicle provides a unique opportunity to demonstrate other fire safety technologies including fire detection, fire suppression, post-fire cleanup and monitoring.
